speaker: GIBSON
text: Good evening from the Field House at Washington University in St.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Louis.

speaker: GIBSON
text: I’m Charles Gibson of ABC News and “Good Morning America.

speaker: GIBSON
text: ” I welcome you to the second of the 2004 presidential debates between President George W.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Bush, the Republican nominee, and Senator John Kerry, the Democratic nominee.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The debates are sponsored by the Commission on Presidential Debates.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Tonight’s format is going to be a bit different.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We have assembled a town-hall meeting.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We’re in the Show-Me State, as everyone knows Missouri to be, so Missouri residents will ask the questions.

speaker: GIBSON
text: These 140 citizens were identified by the Gallup Organization as not yet committed in this election.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Now, earlier today, each audience member gave me two questions on cards like this, one they’d like to ask the president, the other they’d like to ask the senator.

speaker: GIBSON
text: I have selected the questions to be asked and the order.

speaker: GIBSON
text: No one has seen the final list of questions but me, certainly not the candidates.

speaker: GIBSON
text: No audience member knows if he or she will be called upon.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Audience microphones will be turned off after a question is asked.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Audience members will address their question to a specific candidate.

speaker: GIBSON
text: He’ll have two minutes to answer.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The other candidate will have a minute and a half for rebuttal.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And I have the option of extending discussion for one minute, to be divided equally between the two men.

speaker: GIBSON
text: All subjects are open for discussion.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And you probably know the light system by now.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Green light at 30 seconds, yellow at 15, red at five, and flashing red means you’re done.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Those are the candidates’ rules.

speaker: GIBSON
text: I will hold the candidates to the time limits forcefully but politely, I hope.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And now, please join me in welcoming with great respect, President Bush and Senator Kerry.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Gentlemen, to the business at hand.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The first question is for Senator Kerry, and it will come from Cheryl Otis, who is right behind me.

speaker: OTIS
text: Senator Kerry, after talking with several co-workers and family and friends, I asked the ones who said they were not voting for you, “Why?

speaker: OTIS
text: ” They said that you were too wishy-washy.

speaker: OTIS
text: Do you have a reply for them?

speaker: KERRY
text: Yes, I certainly do.

speaker: KERRY
text: But let me just first, Cheryl, if you will, I want to thank Charlie for moderating.

speaker: KERRY
text: I want to thank Washington University for hosting us here this evening.

speaker: KERRY
text: Mr.

speaker: KERRY
text: President, it’s good to be with you again this evening, sir.

speaker: KERRY
text: Cheryl, the president didn’t find weapons of mass destruction in Iraq, so he’s really turned his campaign into a weapon of mass deception.

speaker: KERRY
text: And the result is that you’ve been bombarded with advertisements suggesting that I’ve changed a position on this or that or the other.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now, the three things they try to say I’ve changed position on are the Patriot Act; I haven’t.

speaker: KERRY
text: I support it.

speaker: KERRY
text: I just don’t like the way John Ashcroft has applied it, and we’re going to change a few things.

speaker: KERRY
text: The chairman of the Republican Party thinks we ought to change a few things.

speaker: KERRY
text: No Child Left Behind Act, I voted for it.

speaker: KERRY
text: I support it.

speaker: KERRY
text: I support the goals.

speaker: KERRY
text: But the president has underfunded it by $28 billion.

speaker: KERRY
text: Right here in St.

speaker: KERRY
text: Louis, you’ve laid off 350 teachers.

speaker: KERRY
text: You’re 150 — excuse me, I think it’s a little more, about $100 million shy of what you ought to be under the No Child Left Behind Act to help your education system here.

speaker: KERRY
text: So I complain about that.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’ve argued that we should fully funded it.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president says I’ve changed my mind.

speaker: KERRY
text: I haven’t changed my mind: I’m going to fully fund it.

speaker: KERRY
text: So these are the differences.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now, the president has presided over an economy where we’ve lost 1.

speaker: KERRY
text: 6 million jobs.

speaker: KERRY
text: The first president in 72 years to lose jobs.

speaker: KERRY
text: I have a plan to put people back to work.

speaker: KERRY
text: That’s not wishy- washy.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m going to close the loopholes that actually encourage companies to go overseas.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president wants to keep them open.

speaker: KERRY
text: I think I’m right.

speaker: KERRY
text: I think he’s wrong.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m going to give you a tax cut.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president gave the top 1 percent of income-earners in America, got $89 billion last year, more than the 80 percent of people who earn $100,000 or less all put together.

speaker: KERRY
text: I think that’s wrong.

speaker: KERRY
text: That’s not wishy-washy, and that’s what I’m fighting for, you.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President, a minute and a half.

speaker: BUSH
text: Charlie, thank you, and thank our panelists.

speaker: BUSH
text: And, Senator, thank you.

speaker: BUSH
text: I can — and thanks, Washington U.

speaker: BUSH
text: as well.

speaker: BUSH
text: I can see why people at your workplace think he changes positions a lot, because he does.

speaker: BUSH
text: He said he voted for the $87 billion, and voted against it right before he voted for it.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that sends a confusing signal to people.

speaker: BUSH
text: He said he thought Saddam Hussein was a grave threat, and now he said it was a mistake to remove Saddam Hussein from power.

speaker: BUSH
text: No, I can see why people think that he changes position quite often, because he does.

speaker: BUSH
text: You know, for a while he was a strong supporter of getting rid of Saddam Hussein.

speaker: BUSH
text: He saw the wisdom — until the Democrat primary came along and Howard Dean, the anti-war candidate, began to gain on him, and he changed positions.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t see how you can lead this country in a time of war, in a time of uncertainty, if you change your mind because of politics.

speaker: BUSH
text: He just brought up the tax cut.

speaker: BUSH
text: You remember we increased that child credit by $1,000, reduced the marriage penalty, created a 10 percent tax bracket for the lower-income Americans.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s right at the middle class.

speaker: BUSH
text: He voted against it.

speaker: BUSH
text: And yet he tells you he’s for a middle- class tax cut.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s — you’ve got to be consistent when you’re the president.

speaker: BUSH
text: There’s a lot of pressures.

speaker: BUSH
text: And you’ve got to be firm and consistent.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President, I would follow up, but we have a series of questions on Iraq, and so I will turn to the next questioner.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The question is for President Bush, and the questioner is Robin Dahle.

speaker: DAHLE
text: Mr.

speaker: DAHLE
text: President, yesterday in a statement you admitted that Iraq did not have weapons of mass destruction, but justified the invasion by stating, I quote, “He retained the knowledge, the materials, the means and the intent to produce weapons of mass destruction and could have passed this knowledge to our terrorist enemies.

speaker: DAHLE
text: ” Do you sincerely believe this to be a reasonable justification for invasion when this statement applies to so many other countries, including North Korea?

speaker: BUSH
text: Each situation is different, Robin.

speaker: BUSH
text: And obviously we hope that diplomacy works before you ever use force.

speaker: BUSH
text: The hardest decision a president makes is ever to use force.

speaker: BUSH
text: After 9/11, we had to look at the world differently.

speaker: BUSH
text: After 9/11, we had to recognize that when we saw a threat, we must take it seriously before it comes to hurt us.

speaker: BUSH
text: In the old days we’d see a threat, and we could deal with it if we felt like it or not.

speaker: BUSH
text: But 9/11 changed it all.

speaker: BUSH
text: I vowed to our countrymen that I would do everything I could to protect the American people.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s why we’re bringing Al Qaida to justice.

speaker: BUSH
text: Seventy five percent of them have been brought to justice.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s why I said to Afghanistan: If you harbor a terrorist, you’re just as guilty as the terrorist.

speaker: BUSH
text: And the Taliban is no longer in power, and Al Qaida no longer has a place to plan.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I saw a unique threat in Saddam Hussein, as did my opponent, because we thought he had weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: BUSH
text: And the unique threat was that he could give weapons of mass destruction to an organization like Al Qaida, and the harm they inflicted on us with airplanes would be multiplied greatly by weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that was the serious, serious threat.

speaker: BUSH
text: So I tried diplomacy, went to the United Nations.

speaker: BUSH
text: But as we learned in the same report I quoted, Saddam Hussein was gaming the oil-for-food program to get rid of sanctions.

speaker: BUSH
text: He was trying to get rid of sanctions for a reason: He wanted to restart his weapons programs.

speaker: BUSH
text: We all thought there was weapons there, Robin.

speaker: BUSH
text: My opponent thought there was weapons there.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s why he called him a grave threat.

speaker: BUSH
text: I wasn’t happy when we found out there wasn’t weapons, and we’ve got an intelligence group together to figure out why.

speaker: BUSH
text: But Saddam Hussein was a unique threat.

speaker: BUSH
text: And the world is better off without him in power.

speaker: BUSH
text: And my opponent’s plans lead me to conclude that Saddam Hussein would still be in power, and the world would be more dangerous.

speaker: BUSH
text: Thank you, sir.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: KERRY
text: Robin, I’m going to answer your question.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m also going to talk — respond to what you asked, Cheryl, at the same time.

speaker: KERRY
text: The world is more dangerous today.

speaker: KERRY
text: The world is more dangerous today because the president didn’t make the right judgments.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now, the president wishes that I had changed my mind.

speaker: KERRY
text: He wants you to believe that because he can’t come here and tell you that he’s created new jobs for America.

speaker: KERRY
text: He’s lost jobs.

speaker: KERRY
text: He can’t come here and tell you that he’s created health care for Americans because, what, we’ve got 5 million Americans who have lost their health care, 96,000 of them right here in Missouri.

speaker: KERRY
text: He can’t come here and tell you that he’s left no child behind because he didn’t fund no child left behind.

speaker: KERRY
text: So what does he do?

speaker: KERRY
text: He’s trying to attack me.

speaker: KERRY
text: He wants you to believe that I can’t be president.

speaker: KERRY
text: And he’s trying to make you believe it because he wants you to think I change my mind.

speaker: KERRY
text: Well, let me tell you straight up: I’ve never changed my mind about Iraq.

speaker: KERRY
text: I do believe Saddam Hussein was a threat.

speaker: KERRY
text: I always believed he was a threat.

speaker: KERRY
text: Believed it in 1998 when Clinton was president.

speaker: KERRY
text: I wanted to give Clinton the power to use force if necessary.

speaker: KERRY
text: But I would have used that force wisely, I would have used that authority wisely, not rushed to war without a plan to win the peace.

speaker: KERRY
text: I would have brought our allies to our side.

speaker: KERRY
text: I would have fought to make certain our troops had everybody possible to help them win the mission.

speaker: KERRY
text: This president rushed to war, pushed our allies aside.

speaker: KERRY
text: And Iran now is more dangerous, and so is North Korea, with nuclear weapons.

speaker: KERRY
text: He took his eye off the ball, off of Osama bin Laden.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President, I do want to follow up on this one, because there were several questions from the audience along this line.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Go ahead.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Go ahead.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Well, I was going to have you do the rebuttal on it, but you go ahead.

speaker: GIBSON
text: You’re up.

speaker: BUSH
text: You remember the last debate?

speaker: BUSH
text: My opponent said that America must pass a global test before we used force to protect ourselves.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s the kind of mindset that says sanctions were working.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s the kind of mindset that said, “Let’s keep it at the United Nations and hope things go well.

speaker: BUSH
text: ” Saddam Hussein was a threat because he could have given weapons of mass destruction to terrorist enemies.

speaker: BUSH
text: Sanctions were not working.

speaker: BUSH
text: The United Nations was not effective at removing Saddam Hussein.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Senator?

speaker: KERRY
text: The goal of the sanctions was not to remove Saddam Hussein, it was to remove the weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: KERRY
text: And, Mr.

speaker: KERRY
text: President, just yesterday the Duelfer report told you and the whole world they worked.

speaker: KERRY
text: He didn’t have weapons of mass destruction, Mr.

speaker: KERRY
text: President.

speaker: KERRY
text: That was the objective.

speaker: KERRY
text: And if we’d used smart diplomacy, we could have saved $200 billion and an invasion of Iraq.

speaker: KERRY
text: And right now, Osama bin Laden might be in jail or dead.

speaker: KERRY
text: That’s the war against terror.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We’re going to have another question now on the subject of Iraq.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And I’m going to turn to Anthony Baldi with a question for Senator Kerry.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Baldi?

speaker: BALDI
text: Senator Kerry, the U.

speaker: BALDI
text: is preparing a new Iraq government and will proceed to withdraw U.

speaker: BALDI
text: troops.

speaker: BALDI
text: Would you proceed with the same plans as President Bush?

speaker: KERRY
text: Anthony, I would not.

speaker: KERRY
text: I have laid out a different plan, because the president’s plan is not working.

speaker: KERRY
text: You see that every night on television.

speaker: KERRY
text: There’s chaos in Iraq.

speaker: KERRY
text: King Abdullah of Jordan said just yesterday or the day before you can’t hold elections in Iraq with the chaos that’s going on today.

speaker: KERRY
text: Senator Richard Lugar, the Republican chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, said that the handling of the reconstruction aid in Iraq by this administration has been incompetent.

speaker: KERRY
text: Those are the Republican chairman’s words.

speaker: KERRY
text: Senator Hagel of Nebraska said that the handling of Iraq is beyond pitiful, beyond embarrassing; it’s in the zone of dangerous.

speaker: KERRY
text: Those are the words of two Republicans, respected, both on the Foreign Relations Committee.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now, I have to tell you, I would do something different.

speaker: KERRY
text: I would reach out to our allies in a way that this president hasn’t.

speaker: KERRY
text: He pushed them away time and again, pushed them away at the U.

speaker: KERRY
text: , pushed them away individually.

speaker: KERRY
text: Two weeks ago, there was a meeting of the North Atlantic Council, which is the political arm of NATO.

speaker: KERRY
text: They discussed the possibility of a small training unit or having a total takeover of the training in Iraq.

speaker: KERRY
text: Did our administration push for the total training of Iraq?

speaker: KERRY
text: No.

speaker: KERRY
text: Were they silent?

speaker: KERRY
text: Yes.

speaker: KERRY
text: Was there an effort to bring all the allies together around that?

speaker: KERRY
text: No, because they’ve always wanted this to be an American effort.

speaker: KERRY
text: You know, they even had the Defense Department issue a memorandum saying, “Don’t bother applying for assistance or for being part of the reconstruction if you weren’t part of our original coalition.

speaker: KERRY
text: ” Now, that’s not a good way to build support and reduce the risk for our troops and make America safer.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m going to get the training done for our troops.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m going to get the training of Iraqis done faster.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I’m going to get our allies back to the table.

speaker: BUSH
text: Two days ago in the Oval Office, I met with the finance minister from Iraq.

speaker: BUSH
text: He came to see me.

speaker: BUSH
text: And he talked about how optimistic he was and the country was about heading toward elections.

speaker: BUSH
text: Think about it: They’re going from tyranny to elections.

speaker: BUSH
text: He talked about the reconstruction efforts that are beginning to take hold.

speaker: BUSH
text: He talked about the fact that Iraqis love to be free.

speaker: BUSH
text: He said he was optimistic when he came here, then he turned on the TV and listened to the political rhetoric and all of a sudden he was pessimistic.

speaker: BUSH
text: Now, this is guy a who, along with others, has taken great risk for great freedom.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we need to stand with him.

speaker: BUSH
text: My opponent says he has a plan; it sounds familiar, because it’s called the Bush plan.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re going to train troops, and we are.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ll have 125,000 trained by the end of December.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re spending about $7 billion.

speaker: BUSH
text: He talks about a grand idea: Let’s have a summit; we’re going to solve the problem in Iraq by holding a summit.

speaker: BUSH
text: And what is he going to say to those people that show up at the summit?

speaker: BUSH
text: Join me in the wrong war at the wrong time at the wrong place.

speaker: BUSH
text: Risk your troops in a war you’ve called a mistake.

speaker: BUSH
text: Nobody is going to follow somebody who doesn’t believe we can succeed and with somebody who says that war where we are is a mistake.

speaker: BUSH
text: I know how these people think.

speaker: BUSH
text: I meet with them all the time.

speaker: BUSH
text: I talk to Tony Blair all the time.

speaker: BUSH
text: I talk to Silvio Berlusconi.

speaker: BUSH
text: They’re not going to follow an American president who says follow me into a mistake.

speaker: BUSH
text: Our plan is working.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re going to make elections.

speaker: BUSH
text: And Iraq is going to be free, and America will be better off for it.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Do you want to follow up, Senator?

speaker: KERRY
text: Yes, sir, please.

speaker: KERRY
text: Ladies and gentlemen, the right war was Osama bin Laden and Afghanistan.

speaker: KERRY
text: That was the right place.

speaker: KERRY
text: And the right time was Tora Bora, when we had him cornered in the mountains.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now, everyone in the world knows that there were no weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: KERRY
text: That was the reason Congress gave him the authority to use force, not after excuse to get rid of the regime.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now we have to succeed.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’ve always said that.

speaker: KERRY
text: I have been consistent.

speaker: KERRY
text: Yes, we have to succeed, and I have a better plan to help us do it.

speaker: BUSH
text: First of all, we didn’t find out he didn’t have weapons until we got there, and my opponent thought he had weapons and told everybody he thought he had weapons.

speaker: BUSH
text: And secondly, it’s a fundamental misunderstanding to say that the war on terror is only Osama bin Laden.

speaker: BUSH
text: The war on terror is to make sure that these terrorist organizations do not end up with weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what the war on terror is about.

speaker: BUSH
text: Of course, we’re going to find Osama bin Laden.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve already 75 percent of his people.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we’re on the hunt for him.

speaker: BUSH
text: But this is a global conflict that requires firm resolve.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The next question is for President Bush, and it comes from Nikki Washington.

speaker: WASHINGTON
text: Thank you.

speaker: WASHINGTON
text: Mr.

speaker: WASHINGTON
text: President, my mother and sister traveled abroad this summer, and when they got back they talked to us about how shocked they were at the intensity of aggravation that other countries had with how we handled the Iraq situation.

speaker: WASHINGTON
text: Diplomacy is obviously something that we really have to really work on.

speaker: WASHINGTON
text: What is your plan to repair relations with other countries given the current situation?

speaker: BUSH
text: No, I appreciate that.

speaker: BUSH
text: I — listen, I — we’ve got a great country.

speaker: BUSH
text: I love our values.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I recognize I’ve made some decisions that have caused people to not understand the great values of our country.

speaker: BUSH
text: I remember when Ronald Reagan was the president; he stood on principle.

speaker: BUSH
text: Somebody called that stubborn.

speaker: BUSH
text: He stood on principle standing up to the Soviet Union, and we won that conflict.

speaker: BUSH
text: Yet at the same time, he was very — we were very unpopular in Europe because of the decisions he made.

speaker: BUSH
text: I recognize that taking Saddam Hussein out was unpopular.

speaker: BUSH
text: But I made the decision because I thought it was in the right interests of our security.

speaker: BUSH
text: You know, I’ve made some decisions on Israel that’s unpopular.

speaker: BUSH
text: I wouldn’t deal with Arafat, because I felt like he had let the former president down, and I don’t think he’s the kind of person that can lead toward a Palestinian state.

speaker: BUSH
text: And people in Europe didn’t like that decision.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that was unpopular, but it was the right thing to do.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe Palestinians ought to have a state, but I know they need leadership that’s committed to a democracy and freedom, leadership that would be willing to reject terrorism.

speaker: BUSH
text: I made a decision not to join the International Criminal Court in The Hague, which is where our troops could be brought to — brought in front of a judge, an unaccounted judge.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t think we ought to join that.

speaker: BUSH
text: That was unpopular.

speaker: BUSH
text: And so, what I’m telling you is, is that sometimes in this world you make unpopular decisions because you think they’re right.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ll continue to reach out.

speaker: BUSH
text: Listen, there is 30 nations involved in Iraq, some 40 nations involved in Afghanistan.

speaker: BUSH
text: People love America.

speaker: BUSH
text: Sometimes they don’t like the decisions made by America, but I don’t think you want a president who tries to become popular and does the wrong thing.

speaker: BUSH
text: You don’t want to join the International Criminal Court just because it’s popular in certain capitals in Europe.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: KERRY
text: Nikki, that’s a question that’s been raised by a lot of people around the country.

speaker: KERRY
text: Let me address it but also talk about the weapons the president just talked about, because every part of the president’s answer just now promises you more of the same over the next four years.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president stood right here in this hall four years ago, and he was asked a question by somebody just like you, “Under what circumstances would you send people to war?

speaker: KERRY
text: ” And his answer was, “With a viable exit strategy and only with enough forces to get the job done.

speaker: KERRY
text: ” He didn’t do that.

speaker: KERRY
text: He broke that promise.

speaker: KERRY
text: We didn’t have enough forces.

speaker: KERRY
text: General Shinseki, the Army chief of staff, told him he was going to need several hundred thousand.

speaker: KERRY
text: And guess what?

speaker: KERRY
text: They retired General Shinseki for telling him that.

speaker: KERRY
text: This president hasn’t listened.

speaker: KERRY
text: I went to meet with the members of the Security Council in the week before we voted.

speaker: KERRY
text: I went to New York.

speaker: KERRY
text: I talked to all of them to find out how serious they were about really holding Saddam Hussein accountable.

speaker: KERRY
text: I came away convinced that, if we worked at it, if we were ready to work and letting Hans Blix do his job and thoroughly go through the inspections, that if push came to shove, they’d be there with us.

speaker: KERRY
text: But the president just arbitrarily brought the hammer down and said, “Nope.

speaker: KERRY
text: Sorry, time for diplomacy is over.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’re going.

speaker: KERRY
text: ” He rushed to war without a plan to win the peace.

speaker: KERRY
text: Ladies and gentleman, he gave you a speech and told you he’d plan carefully, take every precaution, take our allies with us.

speaker: KERRY
text: He didn’t.

speaker: KERRY
text: He broke his word.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President?

speaker: BUSH
text: I remember sitting in the White House looking at those generals, saying, “Do you have what you need in this war?

speaker: BUSH
text: Do you have what it takes?

speaker: BUSH
text: ” I remember going down to the basement of the White House the day we committed our troops as last resort, looking at Tommy Franks and the generals on the ground, asking them, “Do we have the right plan with the right troop level?

speaker: BUSH
text: ” And they looked me in the eye and said, “Yes, sir, Mr.

speaker: BUSH
text: ” Of course, I listen to our generals.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what a president does.

speaker: BUSH
text: A president sets the strategy and relies upon good military people to execute that strategy.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Senator?

speaker: KERRY
text: You rely on good military people to execute the military component of the strategy, but winning the peace is larger than just the military component.

speaker: KERRY
text: General Shinseki had the wisdom to say, “You’re going to need several hundred thousand troops to win the peace.

speaker: KERRY
text: ” The military’s job is to win the war.

speaker: KERRY
text: A president’s job is to win the peace.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president did not do what was necessary.

speaker: KERRY
text: Didn’t bring in enough nation.

speaker: KERRY
text: Didn’t deliver the help.

speaker: KERRY
text: Didn’t close off the borders.

speaker: KERRY
text: Didn’t even guard the ammo dumps.

speaker: KERRY
text: And now our kids are being killed with ammos right out of that dump.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The next question is for Senator Kerry, and it comes from over here, from Randee Jacobs.

speaker: GIBSON
text: You’ll need a microphone.

speaker: KERRY
text: Is it Randee?

speaker: JACOBS
text: Yes, Randee.

speaker: JACOBS
text: Iran sponsors terrorism and has missiles capable of hitting Israel and southern Europe.

speaker: JACOBS
text: Iran will have nuclear weapons in two to three years time.

speaker: JACOBS
text: In the event that U.

speaker: JACOBS
text: sanctions don’t stop this threat, what will you do as president?

speaker: KERRY
text: I don’t think you can just rely on U.

speaker: KERRY
text: sanctions, Randee.

speaker: KERRY
text: But you’re absolutely correct, it is a threat, it’s a huge threat.

speaker: KERRY
text: And what’s interesting is, it’s a threat that has grown while the president has been preoccupied with Iraq, where there wasn’t a threat.

speaker: KERRY
text: If he’d let the inspectors do their job and go on, we wouldn’t have 10 times the numbers of forces in Iraq that we have in Afghanistan chasing Osama bin Laden.

speaker: KERRY
text: Meanwhile, while Iran is moving toward nuclear weapons, some 37 tons of what they called yellow cake, the stuff they use to make enriched uranium, while they’re doing that, North Korea has moved from one bomb maybe, maybe, to four to seven bombs.

speaker: KERRY
text: For two years, the president didn’t even engage with North Korea, did nothing at all, while it was growing more dangerous, despite the warnings of former Secretary of Defense William Perry, who negotiated getting television cameras and inspectors into that reactor.

speaker: KERRY
text: We were safer before President Bush came to office.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now they have the bombs and we’re less safe.

speaker: KERRY
text: So what do we do?

speaker: KERRY
text: We’ve got to join with the British and the French, with the Germans, who’ve been involved, in their initiative.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’ve got to lead the world now to crack down on proliferation as a whole.

speaker: KERRY
text: But the president’s been slow to do that, even in Russia.

speaker: KERRY
text: At his pace, it’s going to take 13 years to reduce and get ahold of all the loose nuclear material in the former Soviet Union.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’ve proposed a plan that can capture it and contain it and clean it within four years.

speaker: KERRY
text: And the president is moving to the creation of our own bunker- busting nuclear weapon.

speaker: KERRY
text: It’s very hard to get other countries to give up their weapons when you’re busy developing a new one.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m going to lead the world in the greatest counterproliferation effort.

speaker: KERRY
text: And if we have to get tough with Iran, believe me, we will get tough.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President, a minute and a half.

speaker: BUSH
text: That answer almost made me want to scowl.

speaker: BUSH
text: He keeps talking about, “Let the inspectors do their job.

speaker: BUSH
text: ” It’s naive and dangerous to say that.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what the Duelfer report showed.

speaker: BUSH
text: He was deceiving the inspectors.

speaker: BUSH
text: Secondly, of course we’ve been involved with Iran.

speaker: BUSH
text: I fully understand the threat.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that’s why we’re doing what he suggested we do: Get the Brits, the Germans and the French to go make it very clear to the Iranians that if they expect to be a party to the world to give up their nuclear ambitions.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve been doing that.

speaker: BUSH
text: Let me talk about North Korea.

speaker: BUSH
text: It is naive and dangerous to take a policy that he suggested the other day, which is to have bilateral relations with North Korea.

speaker: BUSH
text: Remember, he’s the person who’s accusing me of not acting multilaterally.

speaker: BUSH
text: He now wants to take the six-party talks we have — China, North Korea, South Korea, Russia, Japan and the United States — and undermine them by having bilateral talks.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what President Clinton did.

speaker: BUSH
text: He had bilateral talks with the North Koreans.

speaker: BUSH
text: And guess what happened?

speaker: BUSH
text: He didn’t honor the agreement.

speaker: BUSH
text: He was enriching uranium.

speaker: BUSH
text: That is a bad policy.

speaker: BUSH
text: Of course, we’re paying attention to these.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a great question about Iran.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s why in my speech to the Congress I said: There’s an “Axis of Evil,” Iraq, Iran and North Korea, and we’re paying attention to it.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we’re making progress.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We’re going to move on, Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President, with a question for you.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And it comes from Daniel Farley.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Farley?

speaker: FARLEY
text: Mr.

speaker: FARLEY
text: President, since we continue to police the world, how do you intend to maintain our military presence without reinstituting a draft?

speaker: BUSH
text: Yes, that’s a great question.

speaker: BUSH
text: Thanks.

speaker: BUSH
text: I hear there’s rumors on the Internets that we’re going to have a draft.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re not going to have a draft, period.

speaker: BUSH
text: The all- volunteer army works.

speaker: BUSH
text: It works particularly when we pay our troops well.

speaker: BUSH
text: It works when we make sure they’ve got housing, like we have done in the last military budgets.

speaker: BUSH
text: An all-volunteer army is best suited to fight the new wars of the 21st century, which is to be specialized and to find these people as they hide around the world.

speaker: BUSH
text: We don’t need mass armies anymore.

speaker: BUSH
text: One of the things we’ve done is we’ve taken the — we’re beginning to transform our military.

speaker: BUSH
text: And by that I mean we’re moving troops out of Korea and replacing them with more effective weapons.

speaker: BUSH
text: We don’t need as much manpower on the Korean Peninsula to keep a deterrent.

speaker: BUSH
text: In Europe, we have massed troops as if the Soviet Union existed and was going to invade into Europe, but those days are over with.

speaker: BUSH
text: And so we’re moving troops out of Europe and replacing it with more effective equipment.

speaker: BUSH
text: So to answer your question is, we’re withdrawing, not from the world, we’re withdrawing manpower so they can be stationed here in America, so there’s less rotation, so life is easier on their families and therefore more likely to be — we’ll be more likely to be able to keep people in the all-volunteer army.

speaker: BUSH
text: One of the more important things we’re doing in this administration is transformation.

speaker: BUSH
text: There are some really interesting technologies.

speaker: BUSH
text: For instance, we’re flying unmanned vehicles that can send real- time messages back to stations in the United States.

speaker: BUSH
text: That saves manpower, and it saves equipment.

speaker: BUSH
text: It also means that we can target things easier and move more quickly, which means we need to be lighter and quicker and more facile and highly trained.

speaker: BUSH
text: Now, forget all this talk about a draft.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re not going to have a draft so long as I am the president.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: KERRY
text: Daniel, I don’t support a draft.

speaker: KERRY
text: But let me tell you where the president’s policies have put us.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president — and this is one of the reasons why I am very proud in this race to have the support of General John Shalikashvili, former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; Admiral William Crowe, former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; General Tony McPeak, who ran the air war for the president’s father and did a brilliant job, supporting me; General Wes Clark, who won the war in Kosovo, supporting me; because they all — and General Baca, who was the head of the National Guard, supporting me.

speaker: KERRY
text: Why?

speaker: KERRY
text: Because they understand that our military is overextended under the president.

speaker: KERRY
text: Our Guard and reserves have been turned into almost active duty.

speaker: KERRY
text: You’ve got people doing two and three rotations.

speaker: KERRY
text: You’ve got stop-loss policies, so people can’t get out when they were supposed to.

speaker: KERRY
text: You’ve got a back-door draft right now.

speaker: KERRY
text: And a lot of our military are underpaid.

speaker: KERRY
text: These are families that get hurt.

speaker: KERRY
text: It hurts the middle class.

speaker: KERRY
text: It hurts communities, because these are our first responders.

speaker: KERRY
text: And they’re called up.

speaker: KERRY
text: And they’re over there, not over here.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now, I’m going to add 40,000 active duty forces to the military, and I’m going to make people feel good about being safe in our military, and not overextended, because I’m going to run a foreign policy that actually does what President Reagan did, President Eisenhower did, and others.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’re going to build alliances.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’re not going to go unilaterally.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’re not going to go alone like this president did.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President, let’s extend for a minute…

speaker: BUSH
text: Let me just — I’ve got to answer this.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Exactly.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And with Reservists being held on duty…

speaker: BUSH
text: Let me answer what he just said, about around the world.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Well, I want to get into the issue of the back-door draft…

speaker: BUSH
text: You tell Tony Blair we’re going alone.

speaker: BUSH
text: Tell Tony Blair we’re going alone.

speaker: BUSH
text: Tell Silvio Berlusconi we’re going alone.

speaker: BUSH
text: Tell Aleksander Kwasniewski of Poland we’re going alone.

speaker: BUSH
text: There are 30 countries there.

speaker: BUSH
text: It denigrates an alliance to say we’re going alone, to discount their sacrifices.

speaker: BUSH
text: You cannot lead an alliance if you say, you know, you’re going alone.

speaker: BUSH
text: And people listen.

speaker: BUSH
text: They’re sacrificing with us.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Senator?

speaker: KERRY
text: Mr.

speaker: KERRY
text: President, countries are leaving the coalition, not joining.

speaker: KERRY
text: Eight countries have left it.

speaker: KERRY
text: If Missouri, just given the number of people from Missouri who are in the military over there today, were a country, it would be the third largest country in the coalition, behind Great Britain and the United States.

speaker: KERRY
text: That’s not a grand coalition.

speaker: KERRY
text: Ninety percent of the casualties are American.

speaker: KERRY
text: Ninety percent of the costs are coming out of your pockets.

speaker: KERRY
text: I could do a better job.

speaker: KERRY
text: My plan does a better job.

speaker: KERRY
text: And that’s why I’ll be a better commander in chief.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The next question, Senator Kerry, is for you, and it comes from Ann Bronsing, who I believe is over in this area.

speaker: BRONSING
text: Senator Kerry, we have been fortunate that there have been no further terrorist attacks on American soil since 9/11.

speaker: BRONSING
text: Why do you think this is?

speaker: BRONSING
text: And if elected, what will you do to assure our safety?

speaker: KERRY
text: Thank you very much, Ann.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’ve asked in my security briefings why that is, and I can’t go into all the answers, et cetera, but let me say this to you.

speaker: KERRY
text: This president and his administration have told you and all of us it’s not a question of when, it’s a question of — excuse me — not a question of if, it’s a question of when.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’ve been told that.

speaker: KERRY
text: The when I can’t tell you.

speaker: KERRY
text: Between the World Trade Center bombing in, what was it, 1993 or so, and the next time was five years, seven years.

speaker: KERRY
text: These people wait.

speaker: KERRY
text: They’ll plan.

speaker: KERRY
text: They plot.

speaker: KERRY
text: I agree with the president that we have to go after them and get them wherever they are.

speaker: KERRY
text: I just think I can do that far more effectively, because the most important weapon in doing that is intelligence.

speaker: KERRY
text: You’ve got to have the best intelligence in the world.

speaker: KERRY
text: And in order to have the best intelligence in the world to know who the terrorists are and where they are and what they’re plotting, you’ve got to have the best cooperation you’ve ever had in the world.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now, to go back to your question, Nikki, we’re not getting the best cooperation in the world today.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’ve got a whole bunch of countries that pay a price for dealing with the United States of America now.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m going to change that.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I’m going to put in place a better homeland security effort.

speaker: KERRY
text: Look, 95 percent of our containers coming into this country are not inspected today.

speaker: KERRY
text: When you get on an airplane, your bag is X- rayed, but the cargo hold isn’t X-rayed.

speaker: KERRY
text: Do you feel safer?

speaker: KERRY
text: This president in the last debate said, “Well, that would be a big tax gap if we did that.

speaker: KERRY
text: ” Ladies and gentlemen, it’s his tax plan.

speaker: KERRY
text: He chose a tax cut for the wealthiest Americans over getting that equipment out into the homeland as fast as possible.

speaker: KERRY
text: We have bridges and tunnels that aren’t being secured, chemical plants, nuclear plants that aren’t secured, hospitals that are overcrowded with their emergency rooms.

speaker: KERRY
text: If we had a disaster today, could they handle it?

speaker: KERRY
text: This president chose a tax cut over homeland security.

speaker: KERRY
text: Wrong choice.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President?

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s an odd thing to say, since we’ve tripled the homeland security budget from $10 billion to $30 billion.

speaker: BUSH
text: Listen, we’ll do everything we can to protect the homeland.

speaker: BUSH
text: My opponent’s right, we need good intelligence.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s also a curious thing for him to say since right after 1993 he voted to cut the intelligence budget by $7.

speaker: BUSH
text: 5 billion.

speaker: BUSH
text: The best way to defend America in this world we live in is to stay on the offense.

speaker: BUSH
text: We got to be right 100 percent of the time here at home, and they got to be right once.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that’s the reality.

speaker: BUSH
text: And there’s a lot of good people working hard.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re doing the best we possibly can to share information.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s why the Patriot Act was important.

speaker: BUSH
text: The Patriot Act is vital, by the way.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a tool that law enforcement now uses to be able to talk between each other.

speaker: BUSH
text: My opponent says he hadn’t changed his position on it.

speaker: BUSH
text: No, but he’s for weakening it.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t think my opponent has got the right view about the world to make us safe; I really don’t.

speaker: BUSH
text: First of all, I don’t think he can succeed in Iraq.

speaker: BUSH
text: And if Iraq were to fail, it’d be a haven for terrorists, and there would be money and the world would be much more dangerous.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t see how you can win in Iraq if you don’t believe we should be there in the first place.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t see how you can lead troops if you say it’s the wrong war at the wrong place at the wrong time.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t see how the Iraqis are going to have confidence in the American president if all they hear is that it was a mistake to be there in the first place.

speaker: BUSH
text: This war is a long, long war, and it requires steadfast determination and it requires a complete understanding that we not only chase down Al Qaida but we disrupt terrorist safe havens as well as people who could provide the terrorists with support.

speaker: GIBSON
text: I want to extend for a minute, Senator.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And I’m curious about something you said.

speaker: GIBSON
text: You said, “It’s not when, but if.

speaker: GIBSON
text: ” You think it’s inevitable because the sense of security is a very basic thing with everybody in this country worried about their kids.

speaker: KERRY
text: Well, the president and his experts have told America that it’s not a question of if; it’s a question of when.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I accept what the president has said.

speaker: KERRY
text: These terrorists are serious, they’re deadly, and they know nothing except trying to kill.

speaker: KERRY
text: I understand that.

speaker: KERRY
text: That’s why I will never stop at anything to hunt down and kill the terrorists.

speaker: KERRY
text: But you heard the president just say to you that we’ve added money.

speaker: KERRY
text: Folks, the test is not if you’ve added money; the test is that you’ve done everything possible to make America secure.

speaker: KERRY
text: He chose a tax cut for wealthy Americans over the things that I listed to you.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President?

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, we’ll talk about the tax cut for middle class here in a minute.

speaker: BUSH
text: But yes, I’m worried.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m worried.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m worried about our country.

speaker: BUSH
text: And all I can tell you is every day I know that there’s people working overtime, doing the very best they can.

speaker: BUSH
text: And the reason I’m worried is because there’s a vicious enemy that has an ideology of hate.

speaker: BUSH
text: And the way to defeat them long-term, by the way, is to spread freedom.

speaker: BUSH
text: Liberty can change habits.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that’s what’s happening in Afghanistan and Iraq.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President, we’re going to turn to questions now on domestic policy.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And we’re going to start with health issues.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And the first question is for President Bush and it’s from John Horstman.

speaker: HORSTMAN
text: Mr.

speaker: HORSTMAN
text: President, why did you block the reimportation of safer and inexpensive drugs from Canada which would have cut 40 to 60 percent off of the cost?

speaker: BUSH
text: I haven’t yet.

speaker: BUSH
text: Just want to make sure they’re safe.

speaker: BUSH
text: When a drug comes in from Canada, I want to make sure it cures you and doesn’t kill you.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that’s why the FDA and that’s why the surgeon general are looking very carefully to make sure it can be done in a safe way.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve got an obligation to make sure our government does everything we can to protect you.

speaker: BUSH
text: And what my worry is is that, you know, it looks like it’s from Canada, and it might be from a third world.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we’ve just got to make sure, before somebody thinks they’re buying a product, that it works.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that’s why we’re doing what we’re doing.

speaker: BUSH
text: Now, it may very well be here in December you’ll hear me say, I think there’s a safe way to do it.

speaker: BUSH
text: There are other ways to make sure drugs are cheaper.

speaker: BUSH
text: One is to speed up generic drugs to the marketplace, quicker.

speaker: BUSH
text: Pharmaceuticals were using loopholes to keep brand — brand drugs in place, and generics are much less expensive than brand drugs.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we’re doing just that.

speaker: BUSH
text: Another is to pass — to get our seniors to sign up to these drug discount cards, and they’re working.

speaker: BUSH
text: Wanda Blackmore I met here from Missouri, the first time she bought drugs with her drug discount card, she paid $1.

speaker: BUSH
text: 14, I think it was, for about $10 worth of drugs.

speaker: BUSH
text: These cards make sense.

speaker: BUSH
text: And, you know, in 2006 seniors are going to get prescription drug coverage for the first time in Medicare.

speaker: BUSH
text: Because I went to Washington to fix problems.

speaker: BUSH
text: Medicare — the issue of Medicare used to be called “Mediscare.

speaker: BUSH
text: ” People didn’t want to touch it for fear of getting hurt politically.

speaker: BUSH
text: I wanted to get something done.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think our seniors deserve a modern medical system.

speaker: BUSH
text: And in 2006, our seniors will get prescription drug coverage.

speaker: BUSH
text: Thank you for asking.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Senator, a minute and a half.

speaker: KERRY
text: John, you heard the president just say that he thought he might try to be for it.

speaker: KERRY
text: Four years ago, right here in this forum, he was asked the same question: Can’t people be able to import drugs from Canada?

speaker: KERRY
text: You know what he said?

speaker: KERRY
text: “I think that makes sense.

speaker: KERRY
text: I think that’s a good idea” — four years ago.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now, the president said, “I’m not blocking that.

speaker: KERRY
text: ” Ladies and gentlemen, the president just didn’t level with you right now again.

speaker: KERRY
text: He did block it, because we passed it in the United States Senate.

speaker: KERRY
text: We sent it over to the House, that you could import drugs.

speaker: KERRY
text: We took care of the safety issues.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’re not talking about third-world drugs.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’re talking about drugs made right here in the United States of America that have American brand names on them and American bottles.

speaker: KERRY
text: And we’re asking to be able to allow you to get them.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president blocked it.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president also took Medicare, which belongs to you.

speaker: KERRY
text: And he could have lowered the cost of Medicare and lowered your taxes and lowered the costs to seniors.

speaker: KERRY
text: You know what he did?

speaker: KERRY
text: He made it illegal, illegal for Medicare to do what the V.

speaker: KERRY
text: does, which is bulk purchase drugs so that you can lower the price and get them out to you lower.

speaker: KERRY
text: He put $139 billion of windfall profit into the pockets of the drug companies right out of your pockets.

speaker: KERRY
text: That’s the difference between us.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president sides with the power companies, the oil companies, the drug companies.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I’m fighting to let you get those drugs from Canada, and I’m fighting to let Medicare survive.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m fighting for the middle class.

speaker: KERRY
text: That is the difference.

speaker: BUSH
text: If they’re safe, they’re coming.

speaker: BUSH
text: I want to remind you that it wasn’t just my administration that made the decision on safety.

speaker: BUSH
text: President Clinton did the same thing, because we have an obligation to protect you.

speaker: BUSH
text: Now, he talks about Medicare.

speaker: BUSH
text: He’s been in the United States Senate 20 years.

speaker: BUSH
text: Show me one accomplishment toward Medicare that he accomplished.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve been in Washington, D.

speaker: BUSH
text: , three and a half years and led the Congress to reform Medicare so our seniors have got a modern health care system.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s what leadership is all about.

speaker: KERRY
text: Actually, Mr.

speaker: KERRY
text: President, in 1997 we fixed Medicare, and I was one of the people involved in it.

speaker: KERRY
text: We not only fixed Medicare and took it way out into the future, we did something that you don’t know how to do: We balanced the budget.

speaker: KERRY
text: And we paid down the debt of our nation for two years in a row, and we created 23 million new jobs at the same time.

speaker: KERRY
text: And it’s the president’s fiscal policies that have driven up the biggest deficits in American history.

speaker: KERRY
text: He’s added more debt to the debt of the United States in four years than all the way from George Washington to Ronald Reagan put together.

speaker: KERRY
text: Go figure.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The next question is for Senator Kerry.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And this comes from Norma-Jean Laurent.

speaker: LAURENT
text: Senator Kerry, you’ve stated your concern for the rising cost of health care, yet you chose a vice presidential candidate who has made millions of dollars successfully suing medical professionals.

speaker: LAURENT
text: How do you reconcile this with the voters?

speaker: KERRY
text: Very easily.

speaker: KERRY
text: John Edwards is the author of the Patients’ Bill of Rights.

speaker: KERRY
text: He wanted to give people rights.

speaker: KERRY

text: You’ve seen co-pays go up, deductibles go up.

text: Everything’s gone up.

text: Five million people have lost their health insurance under this president.

text: I have a plan.

text: I have a plan to lower the cost of health care for you.

text: I have a plan to cover all children.

text: I have a plan to let you buy into the same health care senators and congressmen give themselves.

text: I have a plan that’s going to allow people 55 to 64 to buy into Medicare early.

text: And I have a plan that will take the catastrophic cases out of the system, off your backs, pay for it out of a federal fund, which lowers the premiums for everybody in America, makes American business more competitive and makes health care more affordable.

text: Now, all of that can happen, but I have to ask you to do one thing: Join me in rolling back the president’s unaffordable tax cut for people earning more than $200,000 a year.

speaker: KERRY
text: That’s all.

speaker: KERRY
text: Ninety-eight percent of America, I’m giving you a tax cut and I’m giving you health care.

text: Mr.

speaker: GIBSON
text: President, a minute and a half.

text: Let me see where to start here.

text: And that’s saying something in that bunch.

text: You might say that took a lot of hard work.

text: The reason I bring that up is because he’s proposed $2.

text: 2 trillion in new spending, and he says he going to tax the rich to close the tax gap.

text: He can’t.

text: He’s going to tax everybody here to fund his programs.

text: One percent of America, the highest one percent of income earners in America, got $89 billion of tax cut last year.

text: I want to put money in your pocket.

text: I am — I have a proposal for a tax cut for all people earning less than the $200,000.

text: The only people affected by my plan are the top income earners of America.

text: I both — I heard you both say — I have heard you both say during the campaign, I just heard you say it, that you’re going to cut the deficit by a half in four years.

text: Well, look at the budget.

text: One is make sure Congress doesn’t overspend.

text: But let me talk back about where we’ve been.

text: The stock market was declining six months prior to my arrival.

speaker: BUSH
text: It was the largest stock market correction — one of the largest in history, which foretold a recession.

speaker: BUSH
text: Because we cut taxes on everybody — remember, we ran up the child credit by $1,000, we reduced the marriage penalty, we created a 10 percent bracket, everybody who pays taxes got relief — the recession was one of the shortest in our nation’s history.

text: Senator Kerry, 30 seconds.

text: After 9/11, after the recession had ended, the president asked for another tax cut and promised 5.

text: He lost 1.

text: A $25 billion giveaway to the biggest corporations in America, including a $254 million refund check to Enron.

text: Wrong priorities.

text: You are my priority.

text: Senator Kerry, the next question will be for you, and it comes from James Varner, who I believe is in this section.

text: Mr.

text: Senator Kerry, would you be willing to look directly into the camera and, using simple and unequivocal language, give the American people your solemn pledge not to sign any legislation that will increase the tax burden on families earning less than $200,000 a year during your first term?

speaker: KERRY
text: Yes.

speaker: KERRY
text: Right into the camera.

speaker: KERRY
text: Yes.

text: I am not going to raise taxes.

text: I have a tax cut.

text: And here’s my tax cut.

text: I raise the child-care credit by $1,000 for families to help them be able to take care of their kids.

text: I have a $4,000 tuition tax credit that goes to parents — and kids, if they’re earning for themselves — to be able to pay for college.

text: And I lower the cost of health care in the way that I described to you.

text: Every part of my program I’ve shown how I’m going to pay for it.

text: And I’ve gotten good people, like former Secretary of the Treasury Bob Rubin, for instance, who showed how to balance budgets and give you a good economy, to help me crunch these numbers and make them work.

text: I’ve even scaled back some of my favorite programs already, like the child-care program I wanted to fund and the national service program, because the president’s deficit keeps growing and I’ve said as a pledge, “I’m going to cut the deficit in half in four years.

text: ” Now, I’m going to restore what we did in the 1990s, ladies and gentlemen: pay as you go.

text: We’re going to do it like you do it.

text: The president broke the pay-as-you-go rule.

text: Somebody here asked the question about, “Why haven’t you vetoed something?

text: ” It’s a good question.

text: I think John McCain called the energy bill the “No Lobbyist Left Behind” bill.

text: I mean, you’ve got to stand up and fight somewhere, folks.

text: I’m pledging I will not raise taxes; I’m giving a tax cut to the people earning less than $200,000 a year.

text: Now, for the people earning more than $200,000 a year, you’re going to see a rollback to the level we were at with Bill Clinton, when people made a lot of money.

text: And looking around here, at this group here, I suspect there are only three people here who are going to be affected: the president, me, and, Charlie, I’m sorry, you too.

text: It’s just not credible.

text: You cannot believe it.

text: We’ve got battling green eye shades.

text: And I suspect, given his record, he’s going to raise taxes.

text: Is my time up yet?

text: You looked at me like my clock was up.

text: I think that the way to grow this economy is to keep taxes low, is have an energy plan, is to have litigation reform.

text: 2 trillion just aren’t accurate.

text: Those are the fuzzy math figures put together by some group that works for the campaign.

text: That’s not the number.

text: We’ve got $40 billion going to Bermuda.

text: And third, credible: Ladies and gentlemen, in 1985, I was one of the first Democrats to move to balance the budget.

text: I voted for the balanced budget in ’93 and ’97.

text: We did it.

text: We did it.

text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Mr.

text: President, the next question is for you, and it comes from James Hubb over here.

speaker: HUBB
text: Mr.

speaker: HUBB
text: President, how would you rate yourself as an environmentalist?

speaker: HUBB
text: What specifically has your administration done to improve the condition of our nation’s air and water supply?

speaker: BUSH
text: Off-road diesel engines — we have reached an agreement to reduce pollution from off-road diesel engines by 90 percent.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve got a plan to increase the wetlands by 3 million.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve got an aggressive brown field program to refurbish inner-city sore spots to useful pieces of property.

speaker: BUSH
text: I proposed to the United States Congress a Clear Skies Initiative to reduce sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide and mercury by 70 percent.

text: I have — was fought for a very strong title in the farm bill for the conservation reserve program to set aside millions of acres of land to help improve wildlife and the habitat.

text: We proposed and passed a healthy forest bill which was essential to working with — particularly in Western states — to make sure that our forests were protected.

text: What happens in those forests, because of lousy federal policy, is they grow to be — they are not — they’re not harvested.

speaker: BUSH
text: They’re not taken care of.

speaker: BUSH
text: And as a result, they’re like tinderboxes.

text: And over the last summers I’ve flown over there.

text: And so, this is a reasonable policy to protect old stands of trees and at the same time make sure our forests aren’t vulnerable to the forest fires that have destroyed acres after acres in the West.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve got a good, common-sense policy.

text: Now, I’m going to tell you what I really think is going to happen over time is technology is going to change the way we live for the good for the environment.

text: That’s why I proposed a hydrogen automobile — hydrogen-generated automobile.

text: We’re spending $1 billion to come up with the technologies to do that.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s why I’m a big proponent of clean coal technology, to make sure we can use coal but in a clean way.

text: I guess you’d say I’m a good steward of the land.

speaker: BUSH
text: The quality of the air’s cleaner since I’ve been the president.

speaker: BUSH
text: Fewer water complaints since I’ve been the president.

speaker: BUSH
text: More land being restored since I’ve been the president.

speaker: BUSH
text: Thank you for your question.

text: Senator Kerry, minute and a half.

text: Boy, to listen to that — the president, I don’t think, is living in a world of reality with respect to the environment.

text: Now, if you’re a Red Sox fan, that’s OK.

text: But if you’re a president, it’s not.

text: Let me just say to you, number one, don’t throw the labels around.

text: I’ve been for faith-based initiatives helping to intervene in the lives of young children for years.

text: I was — broke with my party in 1985, one of the first three Democrats to fight for a balanced budget when it was heresy.

text: They’re going backwards on the water quality.

text: I’m going to be a president who believes in science.

text: Mr.

text: And I just told you the facts, sir.

text: The quality of the air is cleaner since I’ve been the president of the United States.

text: And we’ll continue to spend money on research and development, because I truly believe that’s the way to get from how we live today to being able to live a standard of living that we’re accustomed to and being able to protect our environment better, the use of technologies.
